reference.source: WHO Classification of Female Genital Tumours; Blaustein's Pathology of the Female Genital Tract
clinicalPearls: A surface epithelial-stromal ovarian tumour composed of nests of transitional-type (urothelial-like) epithelium set in a dense fibrous stroma; the great majority are benign.
Most benign Brenner tumours are small and discovered incidentally in peri- and post-menopausal women, often within an oophorectomy specimen removed for another reason.
They frequently coexist with other epithelial neoplasms, particularly mucinous cystadenomas, in the same or contralateral ovary.
Characteristic histology shows well-demarcated epithelial nests with longitudinal nuclear grooves (coffee-bean nuclei) and often central microcystic change, with frequent stromal calcification.
Borderline (atypical proliferative) and malignant Brenner tumours are rare; malignancy is suggested by a solid mass with an infiltrative stromal invasion and frank cytological atypia.
The stroma may be hormonally active and occasionally produces oestrogen, so a minority present with post-menopausal bleeding or endometrial hyperplasia.
Immunohistochemistry typically shows the epithelial nests expressing urothelial-type markers such as GATA3, along with p63 and cytokeratins, aiding distinction from other ovarian tumours.
Benign tumours are cured by simple excision or oophorectomy, whereas malignant Brenner tumours are staged and managed like other malignant ovarian epithelial cancers.
reference.pathophysiology: Brenner tumours belong to the surface epithelial-stromal group of ovarian neoplasms and are thought to arise from metaplasia of the ovarian surface epithelium or of Walthard cell nests near the tubo-ovarian junction into transitional (urothelial-like) epithelium. The benign tumour consists of sharply circumscribed nests of bland transitional cells embedded in an abundant, often calcified fibrous stroma. A metaplastic-to-neoplastic sequence is proposed, whereby benign tumours may progress through a borderline (atypical proliferative) phase to malignant Brenner tumour, the last showing stromal invasion, high-grade atypia and, molecularly, alterations distinct from urothelial carcinoma of the bladder. The associated dense stroma can undergo luteinisation and secrete steroid hormones, accounting for the occasional oestrogenic manifestations, and the common coexistence with mucinous tumours reflects the shared metaplastic potential of the ovarian epithelium.
additionalDifferentials: mucinous cystadenoma or borderline mucinous tumour
metastatic urothelial carcinoma to the ovary
high-grade serous or endometrioid carcinoma (for malignant Brenner)
Walthard cell nests and other benign inclusions
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the pelvis to characterise a solid, often calcified mass
CT of abdomen and pelvis when malignancy is suspected for staging
serum CA125 and other epithelial tumour markers
endometrial assessment if there is abnormal or post-menopausal bleeding
immunohistochemistry including GATA3, p63 and cytokeratins
histological search for a coexisting mucinous or other epithelial component
redFlags: a large predominantly solid ovarian mass raising concern for a borderline or malignant Brenner tumour
rapid growth, ascites or extra-ovarian spread suggesting malignancy
post-menopausal bleeding from oestrogenic stromal activity requiring endometrial evaluation
imaging features of stromal invasion or an admixed malignant epithelial component
bilateral or metastatic transitional-type tumour prompting exclusion of a urinary tract primary
reference.prognosis: Benign Brenner tumours have an excellent prognosis and are cured by excision, while borderline tumours behave indolently after complete removal; malignant Brenner tumours are uncommon and their outlook depends on stage, being poorer when disease extends beyond the ovary.
pitfalls: Assuming any solid, calcified ovarian mass is benign without excluding a malignant Brenner tumour on adequate sampling.
Overlooking a coexisting mucinous or other epithelial neoplasm in the same specimen.
Misinterpreting transitional-type epithelium as metastatic urothelial carcinoma without appropriate immunohistochemistry and clinical correlation.
Failing to evaluate the endometrium when an oestrogenic Brenner tumour causes post-menopausal bleeding.
Confusing a cellular fibrous stroma with a sex-cord stromal tumour when the diagnostic epithelial nests are sparsely sampled.

Blaustein's Pathology of the Female Genital Tract, current edition
management: Classify by WHO tier (benign, borderline/atypical proliferative, or malignant) since management is tier driven
Benign Brenner tumour: simple excision or unilateral salpingo oophorectomy is curative, no adjuvant therapy or staging surgery needed once benign histology is confirmed on final pathology

Borderline Brenner tumour: complete surgical removal of the involved ovary, or fertility sparing cystectomy or oophorectomy when fertility preservation is desired, is generally sufficient and chemotherapy is not routinely needed

Malignant Brenner tumour: manage as a malignant epithelial ovarian cancer with comprehensive staging surgery, total hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo oophorectomy, omentectomy, peritoneal staging, and lymph node assessment as indicated

Consider adjuvant platinum based systemic chemotherapy for malignant Brenner tumour with higher stage or high risk disease, following the same stage adapted approach used for other epithelial ovarian cancers
Radiotherapy has no established role in Brenner tumour of any tier
First line for malignant disease is surgical staging or cytoreduction plus adjuvant platinum based chemotherapy when indicated by stage or risk features

For recurrent or progressive malignant Brenner tumour, follow recurrent epithelial ovarian cancer principles, further platinum based or non platinum systemic therapy depending on treatment free interval, with case by case oncology input
Benign disease needs no oncologic surveillance beyond routine postoperative follow up once benign histology is confirmed
Borderline disease warrants periodic clinical and imaging follow up with pelvic examination and ultrasound given the small potential for late recurrence
Malignant disease surveillance follows standard epithelial ovarian cancer protocols combining clinical review, tumour marker trends such as CA125, and imaging as indicated
Refer to gynaecologic oncology before definitive surgery for a solid or complex adnexal mass suspicious for borderline or malignant Brenner tumour on imaging
Refer confirmed malignant Brenner tumour, or stromal invasion or high grade atypia found intraoperatively or on frozen section, for complete staging and consideration of adjuvant therapy

Post menopausal bleeding associated with a Brenner tumour reflects hormonally active oestrogen secreting stroma and warrants endometrial assessment and gynaecology input alongside management of the ovarian mass
